question: A company stores sensitive analytics data in a private S3 bucket. Only an application running on EC2 instances inside a specific VPC should be able to read objects from the bucket; all access attempts from outside that VPC, including from the AWS Management Console using valid IAM credentials, must be denied. A Gateway VPC endpoint for S3 has already been created in the VPC. Which additional step enforces this requirement?

options.A: Attach an IAM policy to every user and role in the account that denies s3:GetObject unless the request originates from the VPC's CIDR range.
options.B: Add a bucket policy statement that denies all S3 actions on the bucket unless the aws:SourceVpce condition key matches the specific VPC endpoint ID.
options.C: Enable S3 Block Public Access on the bucket and rely on the bucket being private by default.
options.D: Configure a security group on the VPC endpoint that only allows inbound traffic from the application's EC2 instances.
options.E: Move the bucket into the VPC using a VPC-only S3 bucket type so it is unreachable from outside.

explanation: A bucket policy with a Deny statement conditioned on aws:SourceVpce (or aws:SourceVpc) is the standard, AWS-documented mechanism to restrict S3 bucket access to requests that traverse a specific VPC endpoint, blocking access from the console, other networks, and other VPCs even with valid credentials.

whyOthersAreWrong.A: IAM policies cannot reliably use source IP/CIDR conditions to distinguish VPC-internal traffic destined for S3 through a Gateway endpoint (there's no source IP to check in that path), and this approach requires maintaining the policy across every current and future principal, which does not scale and is not the standard mechanism for this use case.
whyOthersAreWrong.C: Block Public Access only prevents public/anonymous access; it does not restrict access from authenticated IAM principals outside the VPC, so it does not meet the requirement.
whyOthersAreWrong.D: Gateway VPC endpoints for S3 do not support security groups (that capability applies to Interface endpoints); this option is not technically available for a Gateway endpoint.
whyOthersAreWrong.E: S3 buckets are always Regional, publicly-routable-namespace resources; there is no 'VPC-only bucket type' in Amazon S3.

learningObjective: Architect a reliable and scalable cloud solution using Amazon VPC.

question: A company operates 40 AWS accounts under AWS Organizations. The security team wants a single, centralized location to review CloudTrail events from every account and Region, retained immutably for 7 years, without any member account administrator being able to modify or delete the logs. (Select TWO that together satisfy this requirement.) (This question requires TWO correct answers.)

options.A: Create an organization trail in the AWS Organizations management account with 'Apply trail to all accounts in my organization' enabled, delivering logs to a centralized S3 bucket owned by a dedicated log-archive account.
options.B: Apply an S3 Object Lock configuration in Compliance mode with a 7-year retention period on the centralized log bucket, and use a bucket policy that denies s3:PutBucketPolicy and s3:DeleteObject from all principals except a designated audit role.
options.C: Ask each of the 40 account owners to individually enable CloudTrail in their own account and forward logs via email to the security team weekly.
options.D: Store all CloudTrail logs only in CloudWatch Logs in each member account with a 7-year log retention setting.
options.E: Enable AWS Config in each account independently, since Config natively stores and retains all API activity history for 7 years by default.

explanation: S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode enforces true immutability, preventing even the bucket owner or root user from deleting or overwriting objects until the retention period expires, satisfying the 'cannot be modified or deleted' and 7-year retention requirements.

whyOthersAreWrong.C: This is a manual, unreliable, non-scalable process prone to gaps and human error, and does not provide immutability or true centralization; it is not an appropriate architecture.
whyOthersAreWrong.D: CloudWatch Logs retention can be set very long, but storing logs only per-account fails the centralization requirement, and standard log group permissions do not provide the tamper-proof immutability that Object Lock provides.
whyOthersAreWrong.E: AWS Config records configuration changes and compliance state, not the full breadth of API call/event history that CloudTrail provides, and it does not natively guarantee 7-year retention by default; this option's premise is incorrect.

learningObjective: Architect a reliable and scalable cloud solution using Amazon S3.

question: A company wants its 300 employees to access the AWS Management Console for multiple AWS accounts using their existing corporate Active Directory credentials, with centralized management of which permission sets each user or group can assume in which accounts, without creating individual IAM users in every account. Which solution requires the least ongoing administrative overhead?

options.A: Create an IAM user for every employee in every AWS account they need to access and manage passwords through a shared spreadsheet.
options.B: Set up AWS IAM Identity Center (successor to AWS SSO), connect it to the corporate Active Directory via AWS Directory Service AD Connector, and assign permission sets to AD groups mapped to target accounts within the Organization.
options.C: Configure SAML federation individually between Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS) and each of the 300 employees' IAM users in every account.
options.D: Use AWS Organizations consolidated billing so employees can log in with one shared root account credential.
options.E: Create cross-account IAM roles manually in each account and distribute the role ARNs to employees via email for them to assume using the CLI only.

explanation: IAM Identity Center is purpose-built for exactly this scenario: it federates with an external identity source (via AD Connector or SAML), centrally manages permission sets, and maps them to AD groups and target accounts across the Organization, giving a single sign-on experience with centralized governance and minimal per-account administration.

whyOthersAreWrong.A: Individual IAM users per account per employee is an operational nightmare at this scale, offers no centralized permission management, and using a shared spreadsheet for passwords is a severe security anti-pattern.
whyOthersAreWrong.C: Manually federating AD FS to individual IAM users in every account (rather than centrally through Identity Center/permission sets) is far more complex to set up and maintain and does not scale to 300 users across many accounts.
whyOthersAreWrong.D: Sharing the root account credential violates fundamental security best practices, provides no per-user accountability, and is explicitly discouraged by AWS.
whyOthersAreWrong.E: Manually distributing role ARNs and requiring CLI-only access provides a poor user experience, no console access as required, and no centralized visibility or governance over who has access to what.

learningObjective: Design a resilient architecture meeting strict recovery objectives (RPO/RTO) with AWS IAM.

question: An Amazon Aurora MySQL database stores application credentials that are rotated automatically every 30 days. A Lambda function needs to connect to this database on behalf of end users, but the security team is concerned about connection storms overwhelming the database during traffic spikes, and about credentials being cached by Lambda in a way that breaks after rotation. Which solution addresses both concerns with the least custom code?

options.A: Increase the Aurora DB instance's max_connections parameter significantly and have the Lambda function cache the database password in an environment variable set at deployment time.
options.B: Place Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the Aurora cluster, configure the Lambda function to connect through the proxy endpoint, and configure RDS Proxy to retrieve credentials directly from AWS Secrets Manager.
options.C: Convert the Lambda function into a container running on ECS with a fixed number of long-lived database connections that are never closed.
options.D: Use Aurora Serverless v2 exclusively, since it eliminates the need for connection pooling entirely.
options.E: Configure the Lambda function to open a new TCP connection to the Aurora writer endpoint on every invocation and close it after each request.

explanation: RDS Proxy is purpose-built for this exact Lambda-to-RDS/Aurora pattern: it pools and multiplexes connections so a burst of Lambda invocations does not translate into a burst of new database connections, and it integrates natively with Secrets Manager to always use the current credential, transparently handling rotation without application changes.

whyOthersAreWrong.A: Simply raising max_connections does not solve the fundamental problem of Lambda's concurrency model opening many short-lived connections during spikes, and caching a static password in an environment variable breaks the moment Secrets Manager rotates the credential.
whyOthersAreWrong.C: Rearchitecting away from Lambda to ECS is a major, unnecessary redesign, and long-lived connections that are never closed can themselves become stale or fail after credential rotation, without addressing the connection storm problem for scale-out scenarios.
whyOthersAreWrong.D: Aurora Serverless v2 addresses capacity scaling of the database engine itself, not the connection-management problem created by many concurrent Lambda executions; connection pooling is still needed.
whyOthersAreWrong.E: This is essentially the default (worst-case) behavior that causes the connection storm problem in the first place; opening and closing a new connection per invocation is inefficient and exactly what needs to be avoided.

learningObjective: Architect a reliable and scalable cloud solution using Amazon Aurora.

question: A security team wants to detect and centrally respond to threats such as compromised EC2 instances, anomalous API calls, and potential account compromise across all 40 accounts in their AWS Organization, using native AWS threat detection services with a single pane of glass for findings. (Select TWO services that should be delegated to a dedicated security account as part of this design.) (This question requires TWO correct answers.)

options.A: Amazon GuardDuty, with the security account designated as the delegated administrator and all member accounts configured to auto-enable and send findings to it.
options.B: AWS Security Hub, with the security account designated as the delegated administrator to aggregate findings from GuardDuty, Macie, and Config across all member accounts.
options.C: AWS Trusted Advisor, configured with delegated administration to automatically remediate all compromised resources across the Organization.
options.D: Amazon Inspector, configured as the sole service responsible for aggregating cross-account findings without any other service.
options.E: AWS Health, configured as the primary cross-account threat detection and finding aggregation service.

explanation: Security Hub is designed as the central aggregation and correlation layer for findings from GuardDuty, Macie, Inspector, Config, and third-party tools, and also supports delegated administration for a single Organization-wide view, which is exactly the 'single pane of glass' the team wants.

whyOthersAreWrong.C: Trusted Advisor provides best-practice checks (cost, performance, security, fault tolerance) but is not a threat-detection service and does not perform automatic remediation of compromised resources.
whyOthersAreWrong.D: Inspector performs automated vulnerability assessment of workloads (EC2, ECR images, Lambda) but is not designed as the aggregation point for organization-wide findings across multiple services; it feeds into Security Hub rather than replacing it.
whyOthersAreWrong.E: AWS Health provides visibility into service health and account-specific operational issues, not security threat detection or findings aggregation.

learningObjective: Architect a reliable and scalable cloud solution using Amazon EC2.

question: A public-facing web application behind an Application Load Balancer has recently been targeted by repeated SQL injection attempts and a volumetric Layer 3/4 DDoS attack that caused partial downtime. The company needs protection against both threats and wants AWS to provide a Service Level Agreement (SLA) financial guarantee and 24/7 access to the DDoS Response Team (DRT) during an active event. Which combination of services should be implemented?

options.A: AWS WAF with SQL injection managed rule groups attached to the ALB, plus AWS Shield Standard, which is already enabled by default and provides an SLA.
options.B: AWS WAF with SQL injection managed rule groups attached to the ALB, plus AWS Shield Advanced subscribed on the ALB (and associated Elastic IPs/CloudFront if used).
options.C: Amazon Macie to detect SQL injection patterns, plus AWS Shield Standard for DDoS mitigation.
options.D: Amazon GuardDuty to block SQL injection attempts in real time, plus AWS Network Firewall for DDoS protection.
options.E: AWS WAF for SQL injection protection only, since Shield Standard already includes DRT access and an SLA at no additional cost.

explanation: AWS WAF with managed rule groups (e.g., the SQL injection rule set) directly addresses the SQLi threat, and Shield Advanced adds enhanced DDoS detection/mitigation, cost protection, a financial SLA, and access to the AWS DDoS Response Team, which is exactly what the requirement calls for.

whyOthersAreWrong.A: Shield Standard is automatically enabled at no cost and protects against common, most frequently occurring network and transport layer DDoS attacks, but it does not include a financial SLA or 24/7 DRT access — those benefits require Shield Advanced.
whyOthersAreWrong.C: Macie is designed for discovering and classifying sensitive data in S3, not for detecting or blocking web application attacks like SQL injection; it is the wrong tool for this purpose.
whyOthersAreWrong.D: GuardDuty is a threat detection service, not an inline web application firewall capable of blocking SQL injection payloads, and Network Firewall is a VPC-level stateful/stateless traffic filtering service, not the primary AWS DDoS protection product.
whyOthersAreWrong.E: This is factually incorrect: DRT access and the SLA are Shield Advanced benefits, not part of the free Shield Standard tier.

learningObjective: Architect a reliable and scalable cloud solution using AWS WAF.

question: A company runs EC2 instances in private subnets with no public IP addresses and no inbound security group rules for SSH. Administrators currently use a bastion host in a public subnet to reach these instances, but the security team wants to eliminate the bastion host, remove the need to manage SSH key pairs entirely, and ensure all administrative access is logged centrally for audit. Which solution meets these goals?

options.A: Replace the bastion host with a NAT Gateway, which allows inbound SSH access from the internet securely.
options.B: Use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager, granting IAM permissions to the required users/roles and ensuring the EC2 instances have the SSM Agent and an instance profile with the necessary permissions; enable session logging to CloudWatch Logs or S3.
options.C: Open port 22 to 0.0.0.0/0 on the private instances' security groups so administrators can connect directly from anywhere.
options.D: Distribute a shared SSH key pair to all administrators and rotate it manually every quarter.
options.E: Use AWS Direct Connect exclusively to provide administrators with private network access to the instances, removing the need for any access controls.

explanation: Session Manager provides browser- or CLI-based shell access to instances without requiring any open inbound ports, bastion hosts, or SSH key pairs, while IAM controls who can start sessions and all session activity can be logged centrally to CloudWatch Logs and/or S3 for auditing — meeting every stated requirement.

whyOthersAreWrong.A: A NAT Gateway provides outbound internet access for private subnet resources; it does not provide, and is not designed to provide, inbound SSH connectivity, and would not eliminate key management.
whyOthersAreWrong.C: Opening port 22 to the entire internet is a severe security anti-pattern that dramatically increases attack surface and is the opposite of what the security team wants.
whyOthersAreWrong.D: A shared SSH key eliminates individual accountability, is difficult to rotate securely, and still requires key management overhead — failing multiple stated goals.
whyOthersAreWrong.E: Direct Connect provides private network connectivity from on-premises to AWS but does not by itself provide instance-level access control, authentication, or audit logging, and 'removing all access controls' is a dangerous and incorrect approach.

learningObjective: Architect a reliable and scalable cloud solution using Amazon VPC.

question: A company connects 12 VPCs across 3 AWS accounts to a central AWS Transit Gateway. The security team requires that all outbound internet traffic from every VPC be centrally inspected for malware and intrusion attempts using stateful, signature-based rules before reaching the internet, without deploying and managing inspection appliances in every VPC. Which architecture meets this requirement?

options.A: Deploy AWS Network Firewall in a dedicated inspection VPC attached to the Transit Gateway, route each spoke VPC's outbound traffic through the Transit Gateway to the inspection VPC, and route from there to a NAT Gateway and Internet Gateway.
options.B: Attach an AWS WAF web ACL to the Transit Gateway to inspect all traffic traversing it.
options.C: Enable VPC Flow Logs on every VPC and use Amazon Athena to query for malware signatures in near real time before allowing traffic out.
options.D: Install third-party antivirus software as a required agent on every EC2 instance across all 12 VPCs.
options.E: Use Security Groups with deny rules for known malicious IP ranges, updated manually by the security team as new threats are identified.

explanation: This is the standard AWS centralized inspection architecture: a dedicated inspection VPC with AWS Network Firewall (which supports stateful, signature-based rules including managed intrusion detection/prevention rule groups) attached to the Transit Gateway, with route tables directing spoke VPC egress traffic through it before reaching NAT/IGW — providing centralized inspection without per-VPC appliances.

whyOthersAreWrong.B: AWS WAF operates at Layer 7 for HTTP(S) applications (e.g., attached to ALB, API Gateway, or CloudFront) and cannot be attached to a Transit Gateway to inspect general network traffic.
whyOthersAreWrong.C: VPC Flow Logs record metadata about traffic (IPs, ports, byte counts), not packet payloads, so they cannot be used to detect malware signatures, and querying logs after the fact cannot block traffic before it reaches the internet.
whyOthersAreWrong.D: Host-based antivirus agents address endpoint protection but do not provide centralized, network-level inspection of all outbound traffic and require significant operational overhead to deploy and maintain fleet-wide.
whyOthersAreWrong.E: Manually maintained security group rules cannot perform stateful, signature-based deep packet inspection and cannot scale to keep pace with evolving threats.

learningObjective: Architect a reliable and scalable cloud solution using Amazon VPC.

question: A healthcare company must retain certain S3 objects for exactly 7 years to satisfy regulatory requirements, and no user, including the AWS account root user and administrators with full S3 permissions, should be able to delete or overwrite these objects before the retention period expires, even accidentally. Which S3 feature configuration satisfies this requirement?

options.A: Enable S3 Versioning only, and train administrators not to delete objects manually.
options.B: Enable S3 Object Lock in Governance mode with a 7-year retention period, and grant the s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission only to auditors.
options.C: Enable S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode with a 7-year retention period on the bucket (enabled at bucket creation), which prevents any principal, including the root user, from deleting or overwriting locked object versions until retention expires.
options.D: Configure an S3 Lifecycle policy that transitions objects to Glacier Deep Archive after 7 years to prevent deletion.
options.E: Use IAM policies with explicit Deny statements on s3:DeleteObject for all users to prevent deletion for 7 years.

explanation: Compliance mode is a true WORM (write-once-read-many) control: once applied, the retention period cannot be shortened or removed and locked object versions cannot be deleted or overwritten by any principal, including the root user, until the retention period expires — satisfying the strict regulatory requirement described.

whyOthersAreWrong.A: Versioning alone does not prevent deletion; it just preserves prior versions, but users with delete permissions can still delete both current and previous versions (or the bucket could be emptied), and relying on training is not an enforceable technical control.
whyOthersAreWrong.B: Governance mode allows users with special bypass permissions (s3:BypassGovernanceRetention) to override the retention lock and delete/overwrite protected objects, which fails the requirement that 'no user, including administrators, should be able to' do so.
whyOthersAreWrong.D: Lifecycle transitions change storage class but do not prevent deletion; a Glacier Deep Archive object can still be deleted (subject to standard retrieval considerations), so this does not meet the WORM requirement.
whyOthersAreWrong.E: IAM Deny policies can be modified or removed by anyone with sufficient IAM permissions (including in many cases the root user), so this is not an immutable, enforceable technical guarantee the way Object Lock Compliance mode is.

learningObjective: Architect a reliable and scalable cloud solution using AWS IAM.

question: A cloud platform team wants to allow individual application teams to create their own IAM roles and policies within their AWS accounts for agility, but must guarantee that no team, no matter what policy they author, can ever grant a role permissions broader than a pre-approved maximum set (for example, never allowing iam:*, organizations:*, or access outside approved Regions). Which mechanism should the platform team use to enforce this ceiling on self-authored policies within a single account?

options.A: Service Control Policies (SCPs) attached directly to the IAM roles being created.
options.B: IAM permissions boundaries, set on every role/user the application teams are allowed to create, defining the maximum permissions those identities can ever have regardless of the identity-based policies attached to them.
options.C: Resource-based policies attached to every AWS resource in the account.
options.D: AWS Config conformance packs that alert the platform team after a role with excessive permissions is created.
options.E: IAM group policies applied only to the application teams' human users, not the roles they create.

explanation: Permissions boundaries are specifically designed for this delegated-administration use case: they set the maximum permissions an IAM identity can have no matter what identity-based policy is later attached to it, allowing application teams to create and iterate on their own roles/policies freely while the boundary guarantees they can never exceed the approved ceiling.

whyOthersAreWrong.A: SCPs are attached to AWS Organizations entities (accounts, OUs, or the Organization root), not directly to individual IAM roles; they set account-wide guardrails, not a per-role custom ceiling authored by application teams for roles they create themselves.
whyOthersAreWrong.C: Resource-based policies control access to a specific resource from various principals; they do not cap what permissions an IAM role itself can be granted across all resources and services.
whyOthersAreWrong.D: Config conformance packs are a detective control that reports after the fact; they do not preventively stop an overly permissive role from being created or used.
whyOthersAreWrong.E: Create, which is the actual object of concern in the scenario.

learningObjective: Architect a reliable and scalable cloud solution using AWS IAM.

question: A SaaS provider (Account P) allows its customers to grant the provider's application read access to data stored in the customer's own S3 buckets, in the customer's own AWS account, by having each customer create a cross-account IAM role that the SaaS provider's application assumes. Security researchers warn the provider that a malicious third party could try to trick the provider's application into assuming a role belonging to a completely different, unrelated AWS account (the 'confused deputy' problem) if the customer's trust policy is not carefully scoped. What should the provider require every customer to include in the role's trust policy to mitigate this risk?

options.A: A condition requiring MFA (aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent) on every AssumeRole call.
options.B: A condition on sts:ExternalId set to a unique value assigned by the SaaS provider to that specific customer, which the provider's application must supply on every AssumeRole call.
options.C: A condition restricting the source IP address (aws:SourceIp) to the SaaS provider's published IP range.
options.D: A requirement that the role can only be assumed using long-term access keys, not temporary STS credentials.
options.E: A resource-based policy on the customer's S3 bucket that denies all principals except the provider's root account ARN.

explanation: This is precisely the documented AWS mitigation for the confused deputy problem in third-party cross-account access: each customer's trust policy requires a unique External ID known only to the correct customer/provider pairing, and the provider's application must include the matching External ID on every AssumeRole call, preventing a role from being assumed using a mismatched or reused identifier belonging to another customer.

whyOthersAreWrong.A: MFA is designed for human interactive sign-in scenarios; it is not practical or intended for a third-party service's automated cross-account role assumption, and it does not address the confused-deputy problem of a shared/predictable role ARN being assumed on behalf of the wrong customer.
whyOthersAreWrong.C: Source IP restrictions do not solve the confused deputy problem since the provider's application (the deputy) is the same legitimate caller in every case; the issue is which customer's role/resource it is being tricked into acting on, not where the call originates from.
whyOthersAreWrong.D: STS AssumeRole always issues temporary credentials by design; long-term access keys are not applicable to role assumption and would violate best practices in the opposite direction.
whyOthersAreWrong.E: This addresses S3 bucket-level access but does not solve the underlying cross-account trust relationship problem for the IAM role assumption pattern used by the provider's application.

learningObjective: Architect a reliable and scalable cloud solution using AWS IAM.

question: An ECS task running on Fargate needs access to five non-secret configuration values (such as a feature flag and a log level) and one sensitive database password at container startup. The team wants to minimize AWS costs and use the simplest AWS-native mechanism appropriate to each value's sensitivity, while still injecting all six values into the container as environment variables through the ECS agent (not from within the application). What is the most appropriate design?

options.A: Store all six values, including the database password, as SecureString parameters in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store, and reference all of them in the container definition's 'secrets' field.
options.B: Store the five non-sensitive configuration values as plaintext String parameters in Systems Manager Parameter Store (free of charge) and the database password as a secret in AWS Secrets Manager (with automatic rotation available); reference all six in the container definition's 'secrets' field so the ECS agent resolves them at launch.
options.C: Hard-code the five configuration values directly as plaintext environment variables in the task definition, and store only the password in Secrets Manager.
options.D: Store all six values in Secrets Manager exclusively, since Parameter Store cannot be referenced from ECS task definitions.
options.E: Store all six values in a single Amazon S3 object and have the ECS agent download and parse it at container startup.

explanation: This design matches each value's sensitivity to the most cost-appropriate service: Parameter Store standard (String) parameters are free and simple for non-sensitive configuration, while Secrets Manager (with its native rotation capability) is the better fit for the sensitive database credential; both integrate natively with ECS's 'secrets' field so the ECS agent injects all six as environment variables before the application starts.

whyOthersAreWrong.A: This works technically (Parameter Store SecureString parameters can be referenced from the 'secrets' field), but using SecureString parameters for values that are not actually sensitive adds unnecessary KMS decrypt calls and complexity; it also misses that Secrets Manager offers built-in rotation, which is preferable for a credential like a database password. This is a workable but suboptimal design compared to option B.
whyOthersAreWrong.C: Hard-coding configuration values as plaintext in the task definition is not a best practice for maintainability (values become tied to the task definition revision) even if they are not secret, and this option does not address the requirement to inject them consistently via the ECS agent's 'secrets' mechanism.
whyOthersAreWrong.D: This is factually incorrect: ECS natively supports referencing both AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store parameters and Secrets Manager secrets in the 'secrets' field of a container definition.
whyOthersAreWrong.E: This requires custom application logic to fetch and parse the S3 object, which violates the requirement that injection occur through the ECS agent, and is far more complex and less secure than native secrets integration.

learningObjective: Select the most cost-effective architecture using Amazon ECS to satisfy workload requirements.

question: A Lambda function inside a VPC needs to authenticate to an Amazon Aurora MySQL database without the application ever handling, storing, or retrieving a database password, and the security team wants access to be governed entirely through IAM policies so that credential compromise and long-lived password management are eliminated altogether. Which approach achieves this?

options.A: Enable IAM database authentication on the Aurora MySQL cluster, create a database user mapped to an IAM role/user via the AWSAuthenticationPlugin, and have the Lambda function generate a short-lived authentication token using the RDS 'generate-db-auth-token' capability, granting the Lambda execution role rds-db:connect permission scoped to that database user.
options.B: Store the database password in the Lambda function's environment variables encrypted with a KMS key, and rotate it manually every 24 hours.
options.C: Use AWS Secrets Manager exclusively, which eliminates the need for any IAM permissions since Secrets Manager handles all authentication internally.
options.D: Configure Aurora to accept anonymous connections from within the VPC's CIDR range only, removing the need for a password altogether.
options.E: Use an RDS Proxy configured with 'IAM authentication disabled' so the Lambda function connects using a shared static application password stored in the proxy configuration.

explanation: IAM database authentication is the AWS feature purpose-built for this exact requirement: the database user is mapped to IAM, the Lambda function requests a short-lived (15-minute) auth token signed using its execution role's credentials, and access is governed by an rds-db:connect IAM policy — eliminating static passwords and centralizing authorization in IAM.

whyOthersAreWrong.B: This still relies on a password (a long-lived secret in an environment variable) that must be managed and rotated, which is exactly what the requirement seeks to eliminate, and manual 24-hour rotation is operationally burdensome and error-prone.
whyOthersAreWrong.C: Secrets Manager still stores an actual database password/credential that the application retrieves and uses to authenticate to the database; it improves password management and rotation but does not eliminate password-based authentication or make authorization purely IAM-based the way IAM database authentication does.
whyOthersAreWrong.D: Aurora MySQL does not support anonymous/passwordless connections based solely on network location, and disabling authentication entirely would be a severe security failure, not a valid AWS capability.
whyOthersAreWrong.E: This explicitly disables IAM authentication and falls back to a shared static password, which directly contradicts the stated requirement.

learningObjective: Architect a reliable and scalable cloud solution using AWS IAM.

question: A company must identify all S3 buckets across 25 AWS accounts that contain personally identifiable information (PII) such as credit card numbers and social security numbers, so the security team can apply stricter access controls to those specific buckets. The team wants an automated, managed AWS service to continuously discover and classify this sensitive data rather than writing custom detection logic. Which service should be used?

options.A: Amazon Macie, with the security account set as the delegated administrator to run automated sensitive data discovery jobs against S3 buckets across all member accounts.
options.B: Amazon Inspector, configured to scan S3 bucket contents for PII patterns using its vulnerability scanning engine.
options.C: AWS Config, using a managed rule that flags buckets containing PII based on object metadata.
options.D: Amazon GuardDuty S3 Protection, which classifies object content for sensitive data patterns.
options.E: AWS Trusted Advisor's security category, which includes automated PII discovery for S3 as a core check.

explanation: Amazon Macie is the AWS managed service purpose-built for discovering and classifying sensitive data (including PII like credit card and SSN patterns) stored in S3, and it supports Organizations-wide delegated administration for centralized, automated discovery jobs across many accounts.

whyOthersAreWrong.B: Inspector performs automated vulnerability and network-reachability assessments of compute resources (EC2, ECR images, Lambda code); it does not scan S3 object content for sensitive data patterns like PII.
whyOthersAreWrong.C: Config evaluates resource configuration compliance (e.g., is encryption enabled, is a bucket public); it does not inspect or classify the actual content of objects for PII.
whyOthersAreWrong.D: GuardDuty S3 Protection monitors S3 data plane events (like CloudTrail S3 events) for anomalous/malicious access patterns; it does not perform content-level classification of objects to identify PII, which is Macie's specific role.
whyOthersAreWrong.E: Trusted Advisor provides general best-practice checks around cost, performance, security configuration, and fault tolerance; it does not perform content-based PII discovery in S3.

learningObjective: Architect a reliable and scalable cloud solution using Amazon S3.

question: A company runs a production Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster that stores customer payment metadata. Compliance requires that the data be protected both at rest and in transit, with the database rejecting any client connection attempt that is not encrypted. (Select TWO actions required to fully satisfy this requirement.) (This question requires TWO correct answers.)

options.A: Enable encryption at rest on the Aurora cluster using an AWS KMS key (set at cluster creation, or migrated via snapshot copy/restore for an existing unencrypted cluster).
options.B: Set the DB cluster parameter 'require_secure_transport' to ON (or enforce equivalent SSL/TLS-only settings) so that Aurora MySQL refuses any client connection that does not use SSL/TLS.
options.C: Enable S3 default encryption on the bucket used for Aurora automated backups, since backups are stored independently of the cluster's own encryption setting.
options.D: Rely solely on the VPC's private subnet placement, since traffic within a VPC subnet is automatically encrypted in transit by AWS at the network layer.
options.E: Enable Multi-AZ deployment, since Multi-AZ automatically encrypts all client-to-database connections. (Questions 21–37)

explanation: Enforcing 'require_secure_transport' (or the equivalent SSL-enforcing parameter) ensures the database itself rejects any non-TLS connection attempt, directly satisfying the requirement that unencrypted connections be refused rather than merely making TLS optional.

whyOthersAreWrong.C: Aurora automated backups and snapshots automatically inherit the encryption state of the source cluster when the cluster is encrypted; a separate S3 bucket is not used for automated RDS/Aurora backups, and this option does not address the 'in transit' requirement at all.
whyOthersAreWrong.D: For database connections requires explicit SSL/TLS configuration and enforcement, which this option incorrectly assumes is automatic.
whyOthersAreWrong.E: Multi-AZ provides high availability via a standby replica and synchronous replication; it has no effect on whether client application connections to the database use encryption in transit. (Questions 21–37).

learningObjective: Implement secure architectural controls and access policies with Amazon VPC.

question: A global e-commerce company runs its primary Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster in us-east-1. Following a recent regional service disruption, leadership now requires a disaster recovery capability in eu-west-1 with a Recovery Point Objective (RPO) of under 1 second and a Recovery Time Objective (RTO) under 1 minute for the database tier, while keeping ongoing operational complexity as low as possible. Which solution best meets these requirements?

options.A: Configure an Aurora MySQL cross-region read replica in eu-west-1 using standard asynchronous replication, and manually promote it during a disaster.
options.B: Configure Aurora Global Database with us-east-1 as the primary Region and eu-west-1 as a secondary Region, and use managed planned/unplanned failover, which typically achieves sub-second replication lag and failover in under a minute.
options.C: Set up AWS DMS to continuously replicate data from Aurora MySQL in us-east-1 to a separate RDS MySQL instance in eu-west-1.
options.D: Take a manual snapshot of the Aurora cluster every 5 minutes and copy it to eu-west-1 for restoration during a disaster.
options.E: Enable Multi-AZ on the Aurora cluster in us-east-1 only, since Multi-AZ automatically extends to other Regions during a disaster.

explanation: Aurora Global Database uses dedicated infrastructure to replicate storage-level changes across Regions with typical latency under 1 second, and provides managed failover that AWS states can typically complete in under a minute, directly meeting both the RPO and RTO targets with the lowest operational complexity since AWS manages the cross-region replication.

whyOthersAreWrong.A: A standard cross-region read replica uses Aurora MySQL binlog-based asynchronous replication, which typically has replication lag in the seconds and requires a manual promotion process that does not reliably guarantee under a 1-minute RTO; Aurora Global Database is purpose-built with dedicated low-lag storage-level replication specifically to beat these numbers.
whyOthersAreWrong.C: AWS DMS-based replication introduces additional latency and operational complexity (setting up and monitoring replication tasks) and is not designed to hit sub-second RPO or sub-minute RTO targets for this use case.
whyOthersAreWrong.D: Snapshot copying every 5 minutes yields an RPO measured in minutes at best (and typically much worse, given snapshot/copy duration), which fails the sub-1-second RPO requirement by orders of magnitude.
whyOthersAreWrong.E: Multi-AZ provides high availability within a single Region (synchronous replication to a standby in a different AZ); it has no cross-region capability and does not 'extend' automatically to other Regions.

learningObjective: Design a resilient architecture meeting strict recovery objectives (RPO/RTO) with Amazon RDS.

question: A company runs an application with a primary stack in us-east-1 and a fully provisioned, identical standby stack in us-west-2 that is kept running at all times to allow immediate traffic shift during a regional failure. Health checks continuously monitor the primary endpoint. Which Amazon Route 53 configuration correctly automates the traffic shift to the standby Region when the primary becomes unhealthy, and shifts back automatically once the primary recovers?

options.A: Create a weighted routing policy with both Regions set to a weight of 50, so traffic is always split evenly and disruption is minimized.
options.B: Create a failover routing policy with the us-east-1 record set as PRIMARY (associated with a Route 53 health check on the primary endpoint) and the us-west-2 record set as SECONDARY; Route 53 automatically routes to the secondary when the health check fails and back to primary once it passes again.
options.C: Create a geolocation routing policy that routes United States traffic to us-east-1 and all other traffic to us-west-2.
options.D: Create a latency-based routing policy so that Route 53 always sends users to whichever Region has the lowest network latency at the time of the query.
options.E: Manually update the DNS A record's IP address in the Route 53 hosted zone whenever the operations team detects an outage.

explanation: Failover routing policy is specifically designed for active-passive architectures: it continuously monitors the primary record's associated health check and automatically routes all traffic to the secondary record when the primary is deemed unhealthy, then automatically routes back to primary once its health check passes again — exactly matching the requirement.

whyOthersAreWrong.A: Weighted routing splits traffic by a fixed ratio and is not health-check-aware in a primary/secondary sense by default in the way described; it does not automatically stop sending traffic to an entirely failed Region based on the scenario's described active-passive design intent, making it the wrong policy for automated active/passive failover.
whyOthersAreWrong.C: Geolocation routing directs users based on their geographic location, not based on the health/availability of an endpoint; it would not automatically redirect users away from an unhealthy Region.
whyOthersAreWrong.D: Latency-based routing optimizes for lowest latency, not failover; while it can be combined with health checks to exclude unhealthy resources, it is not the purpose-built failover policy and doesn't match the explicit active-passive designation in the scenario as precisely as the failover policy type.
whyOthersAreWrong.E: Manual DNS updates introduce human delay and error, which defeats the purpose of building automated resilience and does not meet an 'automated' failover requirement.

learningObjective: Architect a reliable and scalable cloud solution using Amazon Route 53.

question: A company's disaster recovery requirements specify an RTO of 10 minutes and an RPO of 5 minutes for a mission-critical application, while keeping steady-state DR infrastructure costs as low as possible. The application consists of an Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances behind an ALB and an Aurora MySQL database. Which DR strategy is most appropriate?

options.A: Backup and restore: take periodic backups and restore them into a new environment only after a disaster is declared.
options.B: Pilot light: keep only the database continuously replicating (e.g., via an Aurora cross-region read replica or Global Database) and core infrastructure defined as code in the DR Region, with the compute/Auto Scaling tier scaled to zero or minimal capacity, then rapidly scale out the ASG and promote the database when a disaster is declared.
options.C: Multi-site active-active: run full production capacity simultaneously in both Regions at all times, with a global load balancer splitting live traffic.
options.D: Warm standby with full production-scale capacity running continuously in the DR Region at all times, identical to the primary Region.
options.E: Do nothing beyond standard Multi-AZ within the primary Region, since Multi-AZ alone satisfies any RTO/RPO requirement.

explanation: Pilot light keeps the data tier continuously replicating (satisfying the aggressive 5-minute RPO) and infrastructure-as-code ready to deploy, while compute resources are kept minimal/idle until needed, striking the right balance between meeting a fairly aggressive RTO/RPO and minimizing steady-state cost compared to warm standby or active-active — matching the stated 'low cost' priority alongside the given targets.

whyOthersAreWrong.A: Backup and restore typically has the longest RTO (often hours) since infrastructure must be provisioned and data restored from scratch after a disaster is declared, which would not reliably meet a 10-minute RTO target.
whyOthersAreWrong.C: Multi-site active-active provides the best RTO/RPO (near zero) but at the highest steady-state cost, since full production capacity runs continuously in both Regions; this exceeds what's needed and directly conflicts with the requirement to minimize cost.
whyOthersAreWrong.D: Warm standby with full production-scale capacity running continuously is more costly than necessary for a 10-minute RTO target; a pilot light approach with rapid scale-out can meet this RTO at meaningfully lower steady-state cost.
whyOthersAreWrong.E: Multi-AZ protects against AZ-level failures within a single Region; it provides no protection against a regional disaster, so it does not satisfy a cross-region DR requirement at all.

learningObjective: Select the most cost-effective architecture using Amazon RDS to satisfy workload requirements.

question: An ECS service running on Fargate with a desired count of 10 tasks across 3 Availability Zones is deployed behind an Application Load Balancer. During a rolling deployment of a new task definition, the team wants to guarantee that at least 80% of the desired task count remains healthy and serving traffic at all times, while allowing ECS to launch extra tasks temporarily to speed up the rollout. Which ECS deployment configuration achieves this?

options.A: Set minimumHealthyPercent to 100 and maximumPercent to 100, forcing ECS to replace tasks one at a time without exceeding the desired count.
options.B: Set minimumHealthyPercent to 80 and maximumPercent to 200, and rely on the ALB's health checks to determine when new tasks are considered healthy before old tasks are drained and stopped.
options.C: Set the desired count to 8 permanently to always keep 80% capacity, then manually add 2 more tasks after every deployment completes.
options.D: Disable the ECS deployment circuit breaker so tasks are never rolled back, ensuring maximum availability during deployment.
options.E: Configure an Auto Scaling lifecycle hook on the ECS service to pause deployments until an operator manually approves each batch of task replacements.

explanation: MinimumHealthyPercent of 80 guarantees at least 80% of the desired count remains healthy throughout the deployment, and maximumPercent of 200 allows ECS to launch up to double the desired count temporarily, letting new tasks come up (and pass ALB health checks) before old tasks are drained — directly matching both stated requirements.

whyOthersAreWrong.A: MinimumHealthyPercent of 100 means ECS cannot take any existing task out of service until a replacement is fully healthy, and maximumPercent of 100 means it cannot launch extra tasks beyond the desired count either, forcing a strictly sequential one-in-one-out replacement (in practice this is often infeasible without extra capacity) — it does not match the requirement to allow temporary extra tasks to speed up rollout.
whyOthersAreWrong.C: Manually adjusting desired count around every deployment is operationally fragile, error-prone, and does not use ECS's built-in deployment configuration designed exactly for this purpose.
whyOthersAreWrong.D: The deployment circuit breaker is a safety mechanism that automatically rolls back a failing deployment; disabling it removes an important resilience safeguard and is unrelated to controlling the minimum healthy percentage during rollout.
whyOthersAreWrong.E: ECS deployment configuration does not use Auto Scaling group lifecycle hooks; that mechanism applies to EC2 Auto Scaling group instance lifecycle events, not ECS service deployments, especially not on Fargate which has no underlying ASG to manage.

learningObjective: Architect a reliable and scalable cloud solution using Amazon ECS.

question: An order-processing microservice occasionally experiences a sudden 10x spike in incoming requests that a downstream payment-processing service cannot handle without becoming overwhelmed and failing requests. The architecture team wants to decouple the two services so that spikes are smoothed out, failed message processing can be retried, and messages that repeatedly fail processing do not block the queue indefinitely. Which design achieves this?

options.A: Have the order-processing service call the payment-processing service synchronously via direct HTTPS API calls with a longer timeout configured.
options.B: Place an Amazon SQS standard queue between the two services, have the payment-processing service consume messages at its own sustainable pace, and configure a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) with a maxReceiveCount so repeatedly failing messages are moved off the main queue after a set number of retries.
options.C: Use Amazon SNS alone to fan out order events directly to the payment-processing service's HTTPS endpoint, without a queue.
options.D: Increase the payment-processing service's EC2 instance size (vertical scaling) to handle any future spike, and remove the queue architecture entirely.
options.E: Configure the order-processing service to buffer requests in local memory and retry direct calls to the payment service every second until they succeed.

explanation: An SQS standard queue naturally buffers and smooths bursty traffic, letting the consumer (payment-processing) pull messages at a sustainable rate rather than being pushed a spike; a DLQ with maxReceiveCount automatically isolates poison-pill messages that repeatedly fail, preventing them from blocking processing of subsequent messages — directly satisfying all three stated goals.

whyOthersAreWrong.A: Synchronous direct calls with a longer timeout do not decouple the services or smooth out load; the downstream service is still hit with the full burst directly and will still become overwhelmed, just with delayed failures instead of immediate ones.
whyOthersAreWrong.C: SNS fanning out directly to an HTTPS endpoint is still a push-based, synchronous-style delivery to the downstream service without a buffer; the downstream service would still be exposed to the full burst, and this does not provide retry/DLQ semantics the way SQS does natively.
whyOthersAreWrong.D: Vertical scaling alone does not guarantee handling of unpredictable future spikes cost-effectively, removing the queue architecture reintroduces tight coupling, and this approach does not address retry or poison-message handling at all.
whyOthersAreWrong.E: In-memory buffering in the order-processing service is not durable (lost on failure/restart), does not scale across multiple instances of the service, and constant retries every second could still overwhelm the downstream service — this is a fragile, non-durable approach compared to a managed queue.

learningObjective: Architect a reliable and scalable cloud solution using Amazon SQS.
